title: Before you wander.
intro: Kathmandu's old temples remain a living centre. Five practices help visitors move through them quietly.

photography.title: Photography
photography.body: Most public temple courtyards welcome cameras. Inner sanctums and active puja do not — phones return to pockets there. Portraits sometimes follow an invitation, and sometimes a quiet refusal. We notice the answer before we lift the camera. Priests in trance, the bereaved at cremations, and the Kumari are not photographed. The Kumari Ghar exterior is fine; the goddess herself is not.

footwear.title: Footwear
footwear.body: Shoes come off at any threshold marked by an offering platform, a row of others' shoes, or a small stone trough. Inside Newari courtyards, the visit continues in socks or barefoot. Outside, shoes return. No one announces the change — we follow the example of the people already there.

silence.title: Silence
silence.body: Temple courtyards keep their own quiet. Drums, bells, and chant come and go; we listen rather than add to them. Phones stay silent. Conversations soften. During puja, the visitor waits at the edge until the priest signals the moment is finished.

sacredObjects.title: Sacred objects
sacredObjects.body: Bells are rung once, gently, on entry. Lamps are lit, not extinguished. Offerings — flowers, rice, tika — stay where they were placed. Statues are touched only on invitation. Circumambulation moves clockwise, with the right shoulder always toward the shrine.

kumari.title: If you accidentally photograph the Kumari
kumari.body: The Kumari is the goddess incarnate. Her family alone photograph her. A tourist's accidental photo is deleted, kept off other devices, kept off social posts. There is no apology to make aloud — only a quiet correction. The image is removed; the visit continues.
